description:
Hi! We’re two ambitious scientists looking to make an interactive tool (fueled by our love of frogs) for the “Lunar Landing Site Navigator” challenge! Our idea is H.A.L.O.sim, a 3D interactive lunar mission planning tool that makes it easy and intuitive to understand when the Sun and Earth will be visible from different landing sites on the Moon. 

“One small step for frog; one big leap for frogkind”
summary:
H.A.L.O.sim (Horizon and Lunar Orbital Simulator) is an interactive lunar mission planning tool that makes it easy and intuitive to understand when the Sun and Earth will be visible from different landing sites on the Moon. Future lunar missions face significant challenges due to extreme terrain, prolonged darkness, and limited Earth-communication windows. Although simulations and data needed to evaluate these conditions exist, accessing and interpreting them often requires significant scientific background and navigating complex science software. 

    H.A.L.O.sim provides a solution to this issue by visualizing the lunar topography and orbital data into intuitive and interactive simulations, allowing users to look at all 9 potential Artemis III landing sites. By making these conditions easy to visualize and compare, H.A.L.O.sim helps users understand the challenges of lunar landings and evaluate how location and time affect operations.

    H.A.L.O.sim also includes a game mode targeted towards younger learners where users can simulate choosing a site to set up a lunar base based on topographical data and collect resources like water ice and lunar regolith. Players are able to use the resources they gather to construct machinery and develop their bases to fly their rocket home. The game also includes tips and information about lunar exploration and resource collection, furthering education and accessibility.
details:
H.A.L.O.sim (Horizon and Lunar Orbital Simulator) is a 3D interactive web application designed to simplify the evaluation of different lunar landing sites by visualizing the relationships between local terrain, solar illumination, and Earth visibility over time. Its main feature is an interactive lunar surface simulation that allows users to explore the 9 candidate landing locations for Artemis III and observe how the Sun and Earth move relative to the local horizon. Users can change the simulated date and time to see when a location gets sunlight, communications from Earth, and how long remains before either body is gone. By combining these visualizations with science-backed metrics, H.A.L.O.sim turns complex scientific calculations into an accessible and intuitive mission planning interface.

The application combines lunar elevation data from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with Sun and Earth positions from Spacecraft, Planet, Instrument, C-matrix, Events (SPICE) ephemerides. Several different LOLA digital elevation models are used to construct a balanced approach to modelling. To account for taller objects outside of the actual candidate landing regions blocking the Sun or Earth, the application loads a model containing data at a 20-meter-per-pixel resolution over the whole 80º to 90º latitude surface of the Moon. However, to achieve a higher degree of detail for topographical features within the regions, the application uses models at a higher 5-meter-per-pixel resolution for each of the 9 candidate regions. This blend allows for high detail and consideration of as much topography as possible while still minimizing lag. H.A.L.O.sim is capable of displaying the data in both a 2D and 3D format, allowing the user to see exactly when and why the Sun and Earth are blocked. Python and JavaScript make up the computational backbone of the visual geometry that defines exactly what can block out the Sun or Earth. H.A.L.O.sim simulates the year 2027 at hourly steps, with a 3-meter panel height (adjustable in explore mode) and 1-degree horizon sampling. It also displays detailed technical metrics, including % sunlight, % mean disk (solar panel) lit, % Earth in view, % both bodies in view, longest night time, longest blackout time, and more. 

H.A.L.O.sim also features a game mode specifically designed for educational purposes. In this game mode, the player makes an emergency landing on one of the Artemis III candidate sites and must choose a specific spot to touch down on. Then, they must gather enough hydrogen fuel to propel their spacecraft and return to Earth. They can achieve this by gathering water ice, which is split into hydrogen and oxygen propellants, and lunar regolith from the area around them, and therefore learn about lunar resources and their potential uses. Although the exact locations of water ice deposits in the South Pole are not known yet, the game assumes that they appear anywhere the Sun never hits, so the concepts are easier to convey. Players send rovers to craters where the Sun doesn’t reach and use the lunar regolith minerals to construct helpful machines that accelerate their base’s collection rate. However, because the rovers use radio signals, they cease functioning when the Earth is blocked, and everything relies on the battery when the Sun is down and “sleeps” when the battery runs out. These features help communicate the importance of choosing a location that has good Sun and Earth exposure to the player. Throughout the game, helpful tips and information pop up on the screen to explain both features of the game and various lunar exploration concepts. 

H.A.L.O.sim’s user experience is uniquely designed with education and concept exposure in mind. The application makes use of creative and colorful resource packs and theming that help illustrate concepts. For example, the Sun/Earth exposure heatmap on the sidebar shows visually how much Sun and Earth exposure each area of the region gets. Users can interact with the initial 3D map of the Moon to visualize and choose their region of choice, and switching from site to site is also very convenient. These fun, interactive, and creative features make H.A.L.O.sim accessible with no aerospace background needed, a huge step up compared to other site evaluation simulators. 

With H.A.L.O.sim, we hope to have created an application that makes the factors that go into choosing a landing location on the Moon much easier to understand, especially in the context of initial education regarding the topic. Although NASA already has precise simulations for how topography and timing affect lighting at different lunar landing sites, H.A.L.O.sim allows people who aren’t familiar with terminology or even aerospace in general to quickly get a grasp of how these factors play into where missions like Artemis III land. The game mode and creative user interface will hopefully spark interest in lunar travel in users and help them understand exactly how impactful and useful America’s return to the Moon will be.

To help design H.A.L.O.sim, we used SI tools to help find information and resources (Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT), code and debug the site (Claude Code, Antigravity), and create the voiceover for our demo video (ElevenLabs).
